newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan braces for protest after partial strike.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan braces for protest after partial strike.

text.p: Pakistani opposition parties and business groups staged a partly effective anti-tax strike on Saturday and an Islamist party said police had rounded up thousands of its supporters to try to disrupt further protests.
The Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) party said the security forces had detained more than 5,500 of its activists to prevent them from taking part in a march on Islamabad planned for Sunday.
Islamabad-based JI spokesman Ovais Qasim, said the party's leader, Qazi Hussain Ahmad, was in hiding. "He is on the move to avoid arrest," Qasim said. "He is being chased by police."
An Interior Ministry spokesman said the JI figure for detainees was exaggerated, but could not say how many people had been seized. He denied that the JI leader was being sought.
"All this fuss is a smokescreen designed to hide what they know will be a failed event," he said.

Three JI members of parliament resigned their seats in the National Assembly (lower house) on Saturday, following the example of Ahmad, who quit his seat last month in an attempt to put pressure on Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto to resign.
Qasim said the party would go ahead with its plans to stage a mass sit-in outside the parliament building as part of its campaign against alleged government corruption.

Paramilitary forces were drafted into the capital, replacing police guarding foreign missions, witnesses said. Police kept the Karachi-Peshawar train in Lahore in an effort to prevent JI activists from reaching Rawalpindi and Islamabad.
Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar on Thursday offered to release all JI detainees if the party agreed to shift the venue of its sit-in to a park in the nearby city of Rawalpindi.

JI rejected the offer as well as a suggestion by President Farooq Leghari that the sit-in be held in Islamabad, but not at parliament, which is close to the presidential palace, prime minister's house, government offices and diplomatic enclave.
Three people were killed and 60 wounded when gunfire broke out during a JI demonstration in Rawalpindi in June.

Many markets and businesses stayed shut in cities across Pakistan on Saturday in response to strikes called by opposition parties led by the Pakistan Muslim League and the Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry, witnesses said.
But what had been billed as a general nationwide strike proved far from total. There was little disruption to transport and many factories and small shops remained open.
In Lahore, stone-throwing protesters burned tyres and effigies of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto in three localities, provoking minor clashes with police. No injuries were reported.

Opposition parties had called the strike in anger at last week's 7.86 percent rupee devaluation against the dollar and harsh economic measures designed to persuade the International Monetary Fund to resume payments of a $600 million standby loan.
An IMF mission led by Middle East Division Chief Antonio Furtado arrived in Islamabad on Saturday and began meetings to review the troubled economy with government officials.
"All things are working towards a resumption of the standby loan," said an economic analyst. "The government has already done most of what it has to do to meet IMF conditions."
The IMF mission must complete its review before the fund can release the third tranche, worth about $80 million, of the stalled standby loan provided in December 1995.
Apart from devaluing the rupee, Bhutto has imposed a tough package, including extra taxes, spending cuts and a 10 percent rise in fuel prices, expected to push up prices in general.
